item.statement: After Portugal stopped making it a crime in 2001 to have any drug for your own use, drug use fell.
item.why: The share of adults who had ever tried a drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100, and use in the past year barely moved. Treatment and other help grew too, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.

quiz.reason: Statement kept (only '2001' moved). The why said drug use 'rose slightly': the lines give ever-tried up from 8 to 12 in 100 and past-year use barely changed, with no 'slightly'. Same fact as n 7.

item.statement: After several months off cocaine, people still score clearly lower on memory tests than people who don't use it.
item.why: In 5 studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months, scores were close to those of people who don't use cocaine. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

quiz.reason: The statement had 21 words and 'lower' had no comparison; it is cut to 19, and the why now names who was compared. Same fact as n 22 from the other side.

item.statement: Given LSD or the drug in magic mushrooms without being told which, most people can't tell which one it was.
item.why: In a 28-person lab study, people named the right drug in most sessions, though they rated the trips alike on most measures.

quiz.reason: Common name in place of 'psilocybin'; the why now says what the study was and keeps 'on most measures'.

item.statement: People who have used LSD or magic mushrooms report more mental health problems than otherwise similar people who haven't.
item.why: In a big US survey, problems were at first glance 2 to 3 times as common, but once other drug use, risk-taking and stressful events were counted, none of 20 measures was higher. People were asked once, so it can't show whether these drugs cause or prevent problems.

quiz.reason: Both wordings were over 20 words (21 and 22) and said 'had' where the lines say 'reported'. Cut to 19 words, the survey moved to the why, and the survey's limit added.
